_comment: Publish-console 'App config' template (deployment defaults, becomes ENCLAVE_CONFIG via configCid). 'volumes' names the attested model volumes the platform attaches (the wasm-manager mounts each at /models/<name> in the guest - no paths here by design). The 'models' catalog is stated in FULL for all four ggml volumes; the retired onnx volume qwen2.5-0.5b is gone from the gpu fleet so its entry is dropped here (the catalog embedded in the wasm keeps it for local dev). qwen2.5-0.5b-gguf sets tokenizer_file to null EXPLICITLY: ENCLAVE_CONFIG merges per FIELD into the embedded catalog, whose entry still points tokenizer_file at the retired onnx volume - omitting the key would keep that stale cross-volume path, null clears it so the re-wrapped volume's own bundled tokenizer.json serves. 122b/9b geometry from the volumes' GGUF headers (qwen35moe/qwen35) + the shared Qwen3.5 tokenizer; both open replies with a <think> block, which the large max_new budgets and rep_penalty 1 (penalties distort long reasoning) are sized for. With rep_penalty at 1 the only things standing between a reasoning model and a degenerate loop are top_k and the repeat_guard, so BOTH are set on every thinking entry: top_k 40 because measurement on the fable 27b ("write a haiku", 1200 tokens) put repeated 10-grams at 36.3% with top_k off and 10.6% at 40, while temperature barely moved it; and repeat_guard 4, a HARD stop that ends a reply once one identical block of tokens has repeated four times. The guard is the one that actually bounds the damage: think_budget only arms inside a force-opened <think> block, so a model reasoning in plain prose (fable does exactly this with thinking off) had no limit at all short of max_new_cap - observed 2026-07-29 as an 80k-token haiku repeating one line. kv_layers counts only the FULL-ATTENTION layers (hybrid models keep no KV in the linear-attention ones) so the app's VRAM pricing - weights + KV at the NODE's window (llama.cpp allocates the whole ENCLAVE_GGML_N_CTX up front, not the app's prompt budget) + ~1.5 GB working set - is honest. The 122b needs >=~50% GPU share; the qwen3.6-27b (arch qwen35 in the GGUF, same hybrid SSM family, kv_layers 16 of 64) needs ~28 GB (17.6 weights + 9.1 KV at the 256K node window + working set) = gpu 0.21; the 9b needs ~12 GB (5.6 weights + 4.3 KV at the 256K node window + working set) = gpu 0.09; under that the app now refuses it cleanly instead of the tenant dying by CUDA OOM mid-compute. qwen2.5-0.5b-gguf runs its full native window (32k = 24576 prompt + 8192 gen cap; the embedded 3072 was sized for the retired onnx guest-memory path - ggml KV lives host-side, and the node's ENCLAVE_GGML_N_CTX 262144 already covers it). think_budget 16384 is set on every thinking model, half of default_max_new: a model that gets stuck in its <think> block re-deriving the same step would otherwise spend the whole 32768-token budget reasoning and answer nothing, so at 16384 the server closes the block itself and the model writes its answer with the remaining half. It is a runaway guard, not a style knob - raise it for work that legitimately reasons longer, drop the key (or 0) to let a model think until max_new. qwen2.5-0.5b-gguf does not reason, so it has none. The fable-fusion 27b ships in TWO quants and 'volumes' attaches the Q4 one, deliberately: both entries describe the same model and geometry, but the Q4 is the one sized for a small share. At the fleet's 176K q8_0 node window (ENCLAVE_GGML_N_CTX 180224) Q4_K_M costs ~26.8 GB to serve (18.5 weights + 6.7 KV including the lazily-created MTP head context + working set) and Q5_K_M ~29.5 GB, against the 35.1 GB a 25% H200 share holds. That margin was not always there: at the old 256K window the Q5 needed ~32.5 GB, and because the MTP head context is created LAZILY on the first speculative session the deployment served, answered /warmup in 100 ms, and then stalled the first real chat request when the head's KV and buffers exhausted what was left (deployment a025ed60, 2026-07-28). Never attach both fable volumes at once: two 27b preloads is ~40 GB of weights before a byte of KV, and the default pick is the largest attached model that fits. Largest attached model serves as the default. qwen3.8-27b-mtp-gguf is the CODE-WORK entry and the first Q6 volume in the catalog: same qwen35 hybrid geometry as the 3.6 MTP 27b (64 trunk layers, kv_layers 17 counting the MTP head's own dense block), but unsloth Dynamic Q6_K_XL instead of Q4_K_XL, because a wrong token in code is a broken program rather than a clumsy sentence. It costs ~34.1 GB to serve at the 176K window (25.9 weights + 6.7 KV including the lazily-created head context + working set), so it wants gpu 0.26-0.27 rather than the 0.19-0.21 the Q4 27b volumes take, and it is the one 27b to attach when it is attached at all. Qwen3.8 ships its MTP head inside the base model, so every quant carries it and draft 'mtp' needs no separate variant; what it does NOT carry is a family-identical tokenizer, because Qwen3.8 adds seven audio/TTS ids (248070-248076) on top of the byte-identical 248044-entry vocab and 247587 merges. Ordinary text tokenizes the same, but the file hash differs, so the cross-model draft gate refuses qwen3.5-0.8b-gguf here and the built-in head is the only draft. max_prompt_tokens + max_new_cap sums to the node window exactly on every 27b entry, and THIS one spends that sum differently from its siblings: 131072 + 49152 rather than 98304 + 81920. Every number on this entry that departs from the others departs for one reason - it is the entry a CODING AGENT drives, over /v1 with its own tools array, and an agent's costs are not a chat user's. Context is what actually runs out (an agent replays a growing transcript of file reads and tool results on every step, and past max_prompt_tokens build_prompt silently drops the oldest turn), while no single step needs an 80k-token reply, so 33k tokens move from the second budget into the first. think_budget 4096 rather than 16384 because on an agent a think budget is priced in WALL CLOCK: at the ~90 tok/s this volume sustains with its MTP head (measured 2026-08-14 over a 5000-token reply, 94% draft acceptance; a short cold-session reply reads far slower because session init lands inside decode_ms), 16384 tokens of reasoning is three minutes before a step's first tool call, and 4096 caps it under one. default_max_new stays at 32768, and cutting it is the one agent tuning that BACKFIRES - think_budget is the runaway guard here, while default_max_new is the OUTPUT ceiling, and an agent's output is a tool call carrying a whole file. One write of a 30 KB source file is ~11k tokens of JSON-escaped content sitting on top of the think block, and when the budget runs out mid-string the call is truncated, tools::parse_calls_for cannot read it, and the CallGate flushes the held block to the client as PROSE - measured 2026-08-14 at default_max_new 16384, where opencode was handed a wall of raw <tool_call> JSON and ran nothing. 32768 less the 4096 think budget leaves room for roughly a 75 KB file, and max_new_cap 49152 is what a client that needs more can ask for. repeat_guard 40 rather than 4 because the guard's period-1 rule (reps x 6 consecutive identical tokens, so 24 at the default) is the exact shape of ordinary generated code - a grid literal like [1,1,1,1,...] trips it, the hard stop lands mid-JSON so the tool call is unrecoverable, and the client is handed finish_reason 'repetition', which no OpenAI client understands. 40 puts the floor at 240 identical tokens, clear of any literal a program legitimately contains, while keeping the backstop (and the ThinkGuard loop rescue it drives) that 0 would remove outright. top_k 20 + temperature 0.6 + top_p 0.95 are Qwen's own thinking-mode numbers, tighter than the 0.7/0.9 the other entries inherit from the top level, because a wrong token inside a tool call is a step that does nothing rather than a clumsy sentence. The other half of serving an agent well is NOT config: a client that declares its own `tools` array now stands the pre-pass router down (see apply_web_search), because a deployment that searches the web and rewrites the user turn behind an agent's back is competing with the agent it is serving.
_search_comment: WEB SEARCH is OPT-IN and OFF here: add a 'search' object to turn it on. ITS HOME SINCE 0.39 IS tools.search, beside the deployment's other external capabilities; this top-level spelling keeps parsing forever (config CIDs are immutable) and tools.search wins when both exist. Everything below applies at either location. Absent means the app never makes an outbound request and the playground hides the control entirely. When present, the playground still starts OFF - people choose an enclave because the conversation does not leave it, so reaching outside is always the user's deliberate act, never a default they inherit. The switch (in the model menu) offers off / auto / always. On 'auto' a SHORT router generation asks the MODEL whether the question needs the web, so 'what changed in Rust 1.90' searches and 'rewrite that shorter' does not - which is how a chat app is expected to behave, and it costs one extra tiny generation per turn. web_search:true still searches unconditionally (the 'always' setting), a message beginning '/search ' forces one, and absent never searches. Either way the APP fetches results over wasi:http before building the prompt - from the deployment's own dedicated egress identity, so the user's question goes to the provider from this enclave rather than from their browser. Be honest about what that costs: the provider learns the query and this deployment's IP, and any page the app fetches learns the IP. It does not learn who asked or anything else in the conversation. PICK THE PROVIDER FOR THE NETWORK, FIRST: a deployment's outbound egress leaves from its own dedicated IPv6 and is IPv6-ONLY, so a provider whose host publishes no AAAA record CANNOT be reached and every query dies as ErrorCode::ConnectionRefused. Measured against a live deployment 2026-07-29: api.exa.ai and serpapi.com connect; api.search.brave.com, google.serper.dev and html.duckduckgo.com are refused. So BRAVE, SERPER, TAVILY, BING AND THE KEYLESS 'ddg' DEFAULT ALL FAIL HERE regardless of the key - use 'exa' (or a searxng instance with IPv6). Check any candidate with `dig AAAA <host>` before wiring it. The same constraint hits fetch_pages, which dials each RESULT site directly: most of the web is IPv4-only, so those fetches fail one by one and the hit keeps only its snippet - which is the other reason to prefer exa, whose results carry page text inline (one round trip, and Exa's own network does the fetching). Fields: provider 'exa'|'searxng'|'brave'|'serper'|'ddg' (default ddg, which is IPv4-only - set this explicitly); endpoint (provider base URL override; REQUIRED for searxng); api_key (the credential - set it through SEALED SECRETS, never here, because the configCid is public on-chain); max_results (default 5); fetch_pages (how many top hits to fetch and read in full, default 0 = snippets only - each one is a serial round trip on the request's critical path, so 2 is the usual sweet spot and 5 is slow); page_chars (text kept per fetched page, default 6000, roughly 1.5k tokens); timeout_s (default 15, applied to connect and first byte). Note on 'ddg': it needs no key, which is why it is the default, but it is HTML scraping and DuckDuckGo rate-limits datacentre egress - a deployment that leans on it will start seeing 'duckduckgo declined the query (HTTP 202)'. Anything load-bearing wants brave/serper with a key, or your own searxng (which can itself run in an enclave, leaving no commercial provider in the path). WIRING A KEY, exactly: (1) get the credential from the provider (exa.ai/api - dual-stack, so it is the one that works from here); (2) put the VALUE in the deployment's SECRETS in the console - they are stored on the relay, off-chain, and injected as env vars at every start; never type the key into this file, which is published on-chain by CID and world-readable (the scripted equivalent is set_secrets with payload {"set":{"EXA_API_KEY":"<key>"}}); (3) reference it BY NAME here, e.g. "search": { "provider": "exa", "api_key": "$EXA_API_KEY", "max_results": 5, "fetch_pages": 2 } - the platform substitutes $NAME/${NAME} in config STRINGS from those secrets at launch, so what goes on-chain is the NAME and never the key; (4) restart the deployment, because config and secrets are both read at start. If the secret is missing the placeholder stays a literal, and the app says so by name instead of posting the string "$BRAVE_API_KEY" to Brave and showing you Brave's 401. Verify a live deployment with GET /search?q=test (provider leg) and GET /search?url=https://example.com (fetch+extract leg); the two fail separately and the probe says which. Both are behind the api_key gate when the deployment sets one - ?url= fetches arbitrary URLs from this deployment's egress identity, so it is not left open where an operator asked for auth. TWO SWITCHES SINCE 0.21.0, not one: web search and image generation used to share a single control, which meant a user who would not send their questions to a search provider also lost the picture generator - two very different disclosures behind one toggle. They are now separate everywhere: 'search.default_on' (default FALSE) and 'image.default_on' (default TRUE), the /chat and /v1 request fields 'web_search' and 'image_gen', and two rows in the playground's model menu. The defaults differ because the disclosures differ: a search sends the user's question to a THIRD PARTY who keeps their own logs, while an image prompt goes to a deployment this operator runs, inside the same fleet, under the same attestation - configuring that endpoint was the opt-in and there is no second party to warn about. An operator pointing 'image.endpoint' at something they do NOT run should set image.default_on false. FIRST-RUN DISCLOSURE: when a provider is configured and the switch is off, the playground asks ONCE, in a dialog that names the provider and states exactly what it learns (the query and this deployment's IP; not who asked, never the rest of the conversation). Either answer is remembered per browser and the question is never repeated. It exists because a switch nobody finds is the same as no feature: people ask a question, get a confidently wrong answer from memory, and conclude the model is bad. Setting search.default_on true skips the dialog entirely, which is the right call only for a deployment whose users already know they are searching. The dialog also CARRIES the "Remember on this device" switch, off like everywhere else, because this app stores nothing in a browser until someone asks it to - which includes the record of having answered this question. Without the switch in reach the dialog would reappear every visit looking like a bug; with it, the subtitle states plainly what turning it on buys ("your answer below is kept, so you will not be asked again") versus leaving it off ("this choice lasts for this tab only"). Both switches are the same one and stay in step.
_image_comment: IMAGE GENERATION, THE ROUTED PATH. Since 0.39 the flattened way to wire pictures is a tools.http entry with result {"image": ...} (see _tools_comment) - that works against ANY generator API and lets the MODEL decide mid-answer. This block is the PRE-PASS path and remains fully supported: it serves turns where tools are off, and the /image command and the router's image verdict answer to it. OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level 'image' object pointing at an image-generator deployment and the SAME router that decides about web search will also decide about pictures (only once the user turns the switch on - it starts off) - "draw me a fox" generates one, "what is impressionism" does not. A message beginning '/image ' (or /img, /draw) forces one and skips the router. Absent means the app never calls an image service AND the model is never told the capability exists, so it cannot promise a picture it has no way to make. Fields: endpoint (REQUIRED - the image-generator's base URL, e.g. "https://<id8>.app.enclave.host"; a full /v1/images/generations path is accepted too); api_key (Bearer, when that deployment sets one - reference a SECRET by name, "$IMAGE_API_KEY", never the literal, because this file goes on-chain); model (a name from the image service's catalog, absent = its default, the largest attached); size (default "1024x1024", snapped to the service's limits); timeout_s (default 180 - a 20B MMDiT at 8 steps on a shared H200 is tens of seconds and queues behind other tenants, so this is the one timeout measured in minutes); max_bytes (default 12 MB, the cap on the response - a PNG comes back base64'd at ~1.4x, and exceeding this is reported honestly rather than handing the browser a truncated image). CONTRACT: POST {endpoint}/v1/images/generations with {prompt, n:1, size, model?} -> {data:[{b64_json, seed?}]}, which is exactly what the sibling image-generator app serves. REACHABILITY: outbound egress is IPv6-only, but an image-generator running as another Enclave deployment is fine - every deployment gets a dedicated IPv6. The bytes come back to the browser INLINE as a data: URI, so the picture never costs the user a request to a second origin and a saved chat still renders offline; the cost is carrying it through the SSE stream and into IndexedDB. The text model never sees the image - it is told one was generated and from what prompt, which is enough to acknowledge it without inventing a description.
_tools_comment: TOOLS are OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level 'tools' object and the model can call HTTP endpoints and MCP servers MID-ANSWER, instead of the app deciding about the web before the turn starts (the 'search' router above). Absent means the model is never told a tool exists and the app never calls one. THE EXECUTED REGISTRY IS THE DEPLOYMENT'S, NEVER THE CLIENT'S: a request may turn the feature off, but it cannot add an entry, change a URL or set a header, because executing a caller's tool would be an open fetcher running with this deployment's egress identity and its secrets. A client-declared OpenAI 'tools: [...]' array is honoured as the PASSTHROUGH instead: those entries are rendered into the prompt and a call to one comes back on the reply as 'tool_calls' for the CLIENT to run, and nothing here ever executes one. Since 0.46 the two lists are offered TOGETHER rather than the client's replacing ours - an agent that brings its own file tools keeps web_search, which is the difference between it looking a fact up and it guessing from memory. The model sees one list and is told nothing about which entry is whose; what routes a finished call is the entry's SOURCE, never its name. A name present in both lists resolves to the CLIENT's and ours is dropped from the list entirely, so a client-supplied name still cannot select a server-executed capability. Per-request switches compose as before: 'web_search': false withholds the web builtins from the merged list too, and tool_choice 'none' withholds everything. Clients switch it on with 'tools': true (or off with 'tool_choice': "none"); the playground gets a Tools switch in the model menu that starts OFF unless default_on says otherwise, for the same reason web search starts off - reaching outside is the user's deliberate act. TRAINED FORMAT, NOT A PROMPT TRICK: the block is rendered in the Hermes/Qwen convention (<tools> signatures in the system turn, <tool_call> to answer in) and is therefore only armed on a 'chatml' model. A llama3/gemma/phi3 entry silently keeps the pre-pass router. Small models are the other half of that caveat: qwen2.5-0.5b will not produce a well-formed call, so check GET /tools and a real turn before leaving it on. Fields: max_calls (how many calls ONE answer may make, default 3 - each is a round trip AND a full re-prefill of the conversation, so this is the cost knob; over budget the model is told once to answer from what it has); timeout_s (per call, default 20); max_bytes (cap on one response before it is looked at, default 256 KB); max_chars (how much of a result the model is actually shown, default 6000 - roughly 1.5k tokens, so one chatty endpoint cannot evict the conversation it was called to help with); default_on (default false); search (THE SEARCH LEG'S HOME since 0.39: the same provider/key/budget object documented in the top-level search comment above lives here, beside the other external capabilities; the top-level spelling still parses forever because config CIDs are immutable, and when both are present this one wins); http (endpoints, below); mcp (servers, below). HTTP entries: name (letters/digits/_/- only, 1-64 chars - a name with a space in it comes back from the model mangled and matches nothing); description (this is the WHOLE user interface - a vague one is why a model calls the wrong tool or none at all); parameters (JSON Schema object for the arguments); url (absolute, may carry {arg} placeholders which are substituted percent-encoded); method (GET default, POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE); headers (reference SECRETS by name, "Bearer $TOOL_KEY", never the literal - this file goes on-chain by CID; an unresolved $NAME is DROPPED and the call fails saying which secret is missing, rather than posting the placeholder and earning a baffling 401); body (JSON template whose "$arg" string values are filled from the arguments; absent on a POST sends the arguments object as-is; the RESERVED names "$images" and "$image" inject the turn's attached pictures as data URIs - all of them, or the first - which is bytes the model could never write into its own arguments, and an entry that asks for them is only offered on turns that actually carry a picture and only when the serving model is not reading them itself); query (send leftover arguments as a query string; defaults true on GET); result (how the JSON response becomes a RESULT: {"image": "<dot path>"} extracts a picture - base64 or a data URI, e.g. "data.0.b64_json" - delivers it to the CLIENT through the same pipeline a routed image uses, and tells the model a picture was made; {"text": "<dot path>"} extracts one field so the model is spared the envelope, falling back to the whole body when the path misses; absent hands the body over as-is; an image-producing entry defaults its own max_bytes to 12 MB, because a picture arrives as megabytes of base64); format (FORMATTING AS A PROMPT: an instruction a short internal pass applies to the response before the model sees it, e.g. "render the results as a numbered list: [n] Title - URL - two-line snippet" - the shaping the bespoke search leg does in code, expressed as configuration, for any API; costs one short greedy generation per call, and a failed pass keeps the raw text); route + route_arg (ROUTING AS A PROMPT: when the tool LOOP is not armed - most commonly a model without the trained chatml call format - a single classifier pass reads the conversation and every entry's route line, answers '<name>: <input>' or NO, and the chosen tool runs with <input> bound to route_arg, defaulting to the entry's sole required parameter; the result folds into the turn exactly as a routed search does, an image result delivers like a routed image, and the user's TOOLS switch still gates the whole pass. Ignored on armed turns, where the description does this job after the model has thought. This is what lets a deployment retire the built-in router verdicts: the same pre-pass, offer list written by the config); sources ({"list": "<dot path to the hit array>", "title": "<path within a hit>", "url": "<path within a hit>"} - citations from any API: the extracted rows feed the same numbered source list a routed search produces, so the [n] markers a format prompt asks for resolve to real links). MCP entries: url (the streamable-HTTP endpoint - stdio is impossible in a wasm component and there is nothing here to run one in); headers; allow / deny (filter the server's tool list); prefix (prepended to every name, so two servers can both offer 'search'); discover (default true) and tools (declare them inline instead). COST OF DISCOVERY, read this before wiring one: the component keeps NO state between requests, so a discovered server costs THREE round trips (initialize, notifications/initialized, tools/list) before the prompt can even be built - every turn. Declare 'tools' inline with 'discover': false when the server's list is stable. REACHABILITY, as ever: outbound egress is IPv6-ONLY, so a tool host with no AAAA record cannot be dialled at all (check with `dig AAAA <host>`); another Enclave deployment is fine, every one gets a dedicated IPv6. WHAT CROSSES: the endpoint sees the ARGUMENTS the model chose and this deployment's egress IP - not the conversation, not the user. The playground shows every call and its arguments above the answer, because that is the part that left. VERIFY A LIVE DEPLOYMENT WITH GET /tools: it resolves the registry exactly as a turn would (dialling any MCP server) and returns what the model would be offered plus any 'notes' - a dropped duplicate, an invalid name, a server that would not answer, a missing secret. GET /tools?call=<name>&args=<json> then runs ONE tool, which separates 'can this deployment see the tool' from 'does the tool work'. Both are behind the api_key gate when the deployment sets one. BUILT-INS: "builtin": ["web_search", "request"] hands the model the search leg as tools instead of having the pre-pass router decide for it. Both are backed by the search block (the place a deployment consents to the model reaching the web at all - and request can SEND data, which deserves that gate more than reading does); request is ONE tool for the whole of HTTP (GET by default, and it reads JSON APIs as-is; POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE with a body). The pre-0.38 names fetch_url and post_url still parse and both resolve to request, so existing on-chain configs keep working unchanged. IMAGE GENERATION AND VISION ARE NOT BUILT-INS: they are ordinary http entries using the generic powers above, so they work against ANY API, not just the sibling apps. The canonical pair, against the siblings: {"name": "generate_image", "description": "Generate an image from a text prompt. It is shown to the user directly; you never see it, so acknowledge it briefly. Pick a size whose shape fits the request: wide for landscapes and banners, tall for portraits and posters, square when nothing argues otherwise.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"prompt": {"type": "string"}, "size": {"type": "string", "enum": ["1024x1024", "1024x768", "768x1024", "960x640", "640x960", "1024x576", "576x1024"], "description": "WxH pixels; omit for square"}}, "required": ["prompt"]}, "url": "${IMAGE_ENDPOINT}/v1/images/generations", "method": "POST", "headers": {"authorization": "Bearer $IMAGE_API_KEY"}, "body": {"prompt": "$prompt", "n": 1, "size": "$size"}, "timeout_s": 180, "result": {"image": "data.0.b64_json"}} (an omitted size is pruned from the body - see below - and the generator applies its default_size; the enum stays inside the deployment's min_size/max_size so no value silently snaps to a different shape) and {"name": "view_image", "description": "Look at the image the user attached and answer one self-contained question about it.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"question": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["question"]}, "url": "https://<reader-id8>.app.enclave.host/v1/vision", "method": "POST", "body": {"question": "$question", "images": "$images"}, "timeout_s": 120, "result": {"text": "answer"}} - swap the url/body/result and the same entries drive any other generator or VLM endpoint. UPSCALING, the same shape against the image-generator app's /v1/images/upscale: {"name": "upscale_image", "description": "Upscale the image the user attached to a higher resolution (Real-ESRGAN). factor 4 quadruples each side (the default), 2 doubles it, 1 cleans the image up at the same size. Call it when the user asks to upscale, enlarge, enhance or sharpen a picture.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"factor": {"type": "integer", "enum": [1, 2, 4]}}}, "url": "https://<generator-id8>.app.enclave.host/v1/images/upscale", "method": "POST", "body": {"image": "$image", "factor": "$factor"}, "timeout_s": 120, "max_bytes": 67108864, "result": {"image": "data.0.b64_json"}} - it reads the attached picture ($image) AND returns one (result.image), so it is offered only on turns with an attachment and its output lands in the client like any generated image; a 4x of a big attachment is tens of MB of base64, which is what the raised max_bytes is for. A declared-but-omitted argument in a body template ($factor here) is dropped from the request, not sent literally, so optional knobs like this cost the model nothing to skip. WHY TOOLS BEAT PRE-PASSES: a pre-pass decides before the model has thought about the question, from four messages of context, and it gets exactly one guess; as a tool the model asks when it finds it needs to, with the query (or prompt, or question) it actually wants, and can ask again after reading what came back. WHAT IT COSTS: a full re-prefill of the conversation per call, against the pre-pass's one short extra generation, which is what max_calls bounds. ARMING A CAPABILITY AS A TOOL TURNS ITS PRE-PASS OFF for that turn, so a deployment never pays for both: web_search silences the router's search verdict; an entry with an image result silences its image verdict; an entry that takes $images stands the delegated-vision pre-pass down (the pictures leave the prompt, the model is told which tool to call to look, and author_query does not run). A typed /image or /search command still beats both deciders, and the LEGACY top-level image/vision_service blocks keep the pre-pass path alive for turns where tools are off. SWITCHES: web_search and request are still the web, so the user's SEARCH switch governs them exactly as it governs the router; off means the tools are not in the registry and the model is never told they exist, which is a stronger guarantee than asking it not to use them. Generic http entries ride the TOOLS switch alone. Sources from a model-initiated search or request reach the client as the same numbered list a routed search produces, so its [1] and [2] resolve; a picture from an image-result tool reaches the playground exactly as a routed one does, and /v1 clients find it in the response's enclave.image (buffered) or an 'enclave-image' SSE comment (streaming). IF YOU TURN THIS ON, fix the system prompt: a prompt that says "you cannot call a search tool" or promises pictures happen by themselves is now false and will fight the tools block. Tell it to call web_search for external facts, request to read or call an API, and your image/vision entries by the names you gave them.
_effort_comment: EFFORT SCALING is OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level (or per-model) 'effort' object and the reasoning budget is sized to the QUESTION instead of every turn getting the same ceiling. A one-line classifier pass rates the turn low/medium/high and think_budget for that turn comes from the matching field. Fields: low (default 512), medium (default 4096), high (default 0 = the model's own think_budget, i.e. no reduction), floor (default 256, the shortest block a misrating may produce). The rating can only ever spend LESS than think_budget, never more. WHAT IT BUYS, precisely: think_budget is a ceiling on a RUNAWAY, not a target - a model that reasons for 200 tokens and answers is untouched by any of these numbers. What changes is how long a model that will not stop gets before the block is closed for it: seconds on a greeting instead of the better part of a minute. WHAT IT COSTS: one short greedy generation before the answer starts. FREE when web search is on 'auto', because the same pass that decides about search answers both questions at once; otherwise it is a real round trip on the critical path - measured at +6.4s per turn against a 9B on CPU, and a fraction of a second on a GPU share. THE RATING IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE MODEL: measured 2026-07-30, qwen3.5-9b rated a spread of seven questions the way a person would (greetings and translation low, a linked-list function medium, a proof and a concurrency bug high), while qwen2.5-0.5b rated nearly everything 'high' - on a small model the feature costs a pass and changes nothing, so check the 'effort' field in a reply's enclave stats before leaving it on. An unrated turn (a model that ignores the format, a failed pass) silently keeps the flat think_budget, so this can never be the reason an answer fails.
_vision_comment: VISION (images IN, the opposite direction from the image-generation block above) is a MODEL property, not a deployment switch: a model can read pictures when its volume carries a vision projector beside the weights (any *mmproj*.gguf; the host finds it by that name) and its catalog entry sets "vision": true. Nothing else turns it on, and nothing turns it on for a model that cannot do it - the flag only tells the app to OFFER the capability, and the host is asked again at request time (a node whose llama.cpp toolchain predates vision reports none, and the turn fails saying exactly that instead of quietly ignoring the picture). The playground follows the SELECTED model: the attach button (and paste, and drag-and-drop) appears for a vision model and disappears for a text-only one, so switching models visibly gains or loses the capability. Pictures are resized in the BROWSER to ~1.15 MP before upload, and the /v1 API takes the standard OpenAI content-parts array ({"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}}; the Responses and Anthropic spellings are accepted too). Remote image URLs are REFUSED rather than fetched: resolving one would tell a third-party host what this deployment is looking at, which is the thing running the model in an enclave exists to prevent - and egress here is IPv6-only anyway, so most such fetches would fail confusingly. Fields, all optional: vision (the flag itself, default false); image_tokens (what ONE image is BUDGETED at against max_prompt_tokens, default 1024 - admission control only, the host reports the true cost per image in the reply's stats and the playground shows it in the meta line); max_image_bytes (per image after the browser's resize, default 6 MB); max_images (per REQUEST across all turns, default 4 - each one costs a vision-encoder pass and its own slice of the KV window, and the playground carries only the most recent that many so a long chat never becomes unanswerable). SIZING, the part that bites: the app prices a vision model's projector into its VRAM budget (GET /models shows `fits`), because the projector loads LAZILY on the first image - a deployment that fits the language model alone would serve text happily and then die on the first picture, and a CUDA OOM inside compute aborts the whole tenant. Note also that Qwen3-VL is DENSE (every layer holds KV, unlike the hybrid qwen3.5/3.6 entries with their kv_layers), so at the node's window its KV cache is the dominant cost - price the share for it. NON-CAUSAL MODELS: gemma-style VLMs decode an image with a non-causal mask, which requires the whole image inside one physical batch; on such a model the node needs ENCLAVE_GGML_N_UBATCH >= the image's token count or the app refuses the turn with a message naming that variable (rather than answering from a wrongly-masked image). Qwen3-VL is causal and needs none of that, which is the other reason it is the entry below.
_vision_service_comment: VISION BY DELEGATION, THE PRE-PASS PATH. Since 0.39 the flattened way to wire vision is a tools.http entry whose body template takes "$images" (see _tools_comment) - that works against ANY VLM endpoint and the MODEL asks its own question mid-answer. This block remains fully supported: it serves turns where tools are off, with the authored-question pre-pass below. OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level 'vision_service' object pointing at an image-reader deployment (the sibling app in this repo) and EVERY model this deployment serves can be sent a picture, whether or not its own volume carries a projector. The image goes to that deployment and comes back as prose, which this app folds into the turn it is about to answer. That is the alternative to the per-model 'vision' flag above, and the two are exclusive per turn: a request that NAMES a vision model (e.g. "model": "qwen3-vl-8b") reads the picture locally, and everything else prefers the service when one is configured. WHY DELEGATE: the chat model and the vision model have different lifecycles and different VRAM shapes, and splitting them lets the eyes be started, stopped, resized or upgraded without touching the chat everyone is using - and lets the chat model be the biggest thing the share can hold instead of sharing it with a second set of weights and a second dense KV window. WHAT CROSSES, which is the whole design: not the conversation. One request carries the image bytes and ONE QUESTION, and that question is written by THIS deployment's own model after reading the conversation ('author_query', on by default, one short greedy generation) - so the detail the answer turns on travels as part of the question rather than as a transcript. The user is shown what was asked on their behalf (the /chat stream's {"vision":{...}} event, 'enclave.vision' on /v1, and the reply's meta line). The look is SINGLE-SHOT: the render path is one pass, not a tool-call loop, so the authored question asks for the specific answer AND enough surrounding description to survive the obvious follow-up; when that is not enough the next turn re-queries with the user's new question. Fields: endpoint (REQUIRED, the image-reader base URL; a full /v1/vision path is accepted too); api_key (Bearer - reference a SECRET by name, "$VISION_API_KEY", never the literal, because this file goes on-chain by CID); model (a name from that deployment's catalog, absent = its default); timeout_s (default 120 - a cold VLM session plus an encoder pass can queue behind another tenant, and this sits on a chat turn's critical path); max_bytes (cap on the reply, default 512 KB - it is prose, not pixels); max_images (how many of the turn's pictures to send, default 2); max_answer_chars (how much of the report is folded in, default 6000, so a long description cannot push the conversation out of the window); author_query (default true); prefer_local (default false - set true to let a vision-capable serving model read the picture itself and keep the service for the models that cannot). REACHABILITY, check it FIRST: a deployment's outbound egress is IPv6-ONLY, so app-to-app depends on the gateway answering over v6 for the target name (as of 2026-07-29 the wildcard *.app.enclave.host does publish an AAAA, 2a01:4f9:c013:9b52::1, beside its A). Test the exact path with no inference in the way: GET /search?url=https://<reader-id8>.app.enclave.host/ping on THIS deployment. A failure there is a failure of the vision leg too, and the leg reports the platform's own egress diagnosis rather than "vision failed".
_sso_comment: SIGN IN WITH ENCLAVE is OPT-IN and OFF here: add a top-level 'sso' object and the playground asks visitors to sign in with their Enclave account (the same passkey or wallet they use on enclave.host) before the two generation routes answer. The flow: the playground sends the visitor to {authorize_url}?aud=<this deployment's id>&redirect_uri=<the page>&state=<nonce>; enclave.host authenticates them however it already does, validates that redirect_uri really belongs to the aud deployment, and redirects back with a short-lived signed token in the URL FRAGMENT; every /chat and /title request then carries it as Authorization: Bearer, and the ENCLAVE verifies it - signature against 'signer', audience against 'audience', expiry against the clock - with no outbound call and no session state (see sso.rs; PLATFORM-sso.md is the platform half of the contract). /v1/* accepts a valid token beside api_key, so one login covers the API too. Fields: signer (REQUIRED - the platform SSO signing ADDRESS, 0x+40 hex, published at https://enclave.host/.well-known/sso-signer.json; not a secret, it is the pin, and rotation is a config update here); audience (REQUIRED - THIS deployment's bytes32 id, 0x+64 hex; a token minted for a different deployment is refused no matter how valid its signature, which is the whole point of the field - set it right after the create transaction names the id); authorize_url (default https://enclave.host/sso/authorize); required (default true - false gates NOTHING and merely offers the sign-in link in the sidebar, for a deployment that wants the identity without the door); skew_secs (default 300, clock-drift tolerance on iat only; expiry is strict because it is the only revocation a stateless verifier has). WHAT STAYS OPEN with required=true, deliberately: GET / serves the page that carries the sign-in button, /models is how that page learns authorize_url and aud, and /attestation stays readable because deciding whether to trust this app with a login is exactly when someone verifies it. WHAT THE APP LEARNS: the visitor's wallet ADDRESS (the token's sub), per request, verified. It stores nothing - no session table, no user record - so 'what we store about you: nothing' stays true; the legal page states the sign-in case in those words. WHAT THE PLATFORM LEARNS: that someone signed in to use THIS deployment (it mints the token), which it effectively knew already from serving the login. It does NOT see conversations, which never leave the enclave. NOTE the gate is AUTHENTICATION, not authorization: any Enclave account satisfies it. Restricting WHO gets in (an allowlist of addresses, a token-gated community) is a natural next step but is not built - it would be an 'allow' list of addresses beside 'signer' and one more check in sso.rs.
